claim: Muravyev-Pearson (37 US stocks + 2 ETFs, Apr 2003-Oct 2006, tick data; all maturities, option-alone trades, effective-spread measure, not a strategy return): average quoted spread 8.1 cents per unit, conventional effective spread 6.2 cents, adjusted effective spread about half the quoted spread; timed trades 1.3 cents. Sample ends before 2015.
quote: On average, the adjusted effective spread is two thirds of the conventionally measured effective spread and only about half the quoted bid-ask spread.
title: CXO Advisory summary of Muravyev & Pearson 'Option Trading Costs Are Lower Than You Think' (2015)

claim: Same study: traders who cannot time option trades pay the conventional effective spread (6.2 cents vs 8.1 quoted, i.e. about 77% of the quote; 2003-2006 sample, ends before 2015), so a retail backtest should not assume the low timed-trade cost. Original paper PDF not cacheable (secondary summary).
quote: However, investors who are unable to time option trades bear on average the conventionally measured effective spreads.
title: CXO Advisory summary of Muravyev & Pearson (2015)

claim: Christoffersen-Goyenko-Jacobs-Karoui (341 S&P 500 component stocks, 1996-2007, ends before 2015; end-of-day quoted midpoints, option-alone returns, no costs in the returns): average quoted spread relative to midpoint is 34% for short-term (20-70 day) OTM calls and 23% for long-term (71-180 day) OTM calls; OTM less liquid than ATM, ATM less than ITM.
quote: the average bid-ask spread relative to midpoint of short-term (long-term) OTM calls is 34% (23%).
title: CXO Advisory summary of Christoffersen et al. 'Illiquidity Premia in the Equity Options Market'

claim: Same study: because returns are computed from end-of-day quoted midpoints, they exclude spread cost; illiquid options earn higher gross returns (2 sd rise in illiquidity of short-term OTM calls goes with 2.4% higher next-day gross return, 1996-2007), which the summary reads as compensation for friction, so midpoint-fill backtests overstate buyer returns most on illiquid contracts.
quote: In summary, evidence suggests that low-cost traders may be able to extract an illiquidity premium from equity options, but perhaps more realistically indicates that the premium counterbalances trading friction for option buyers.
title: CXO Advisory summary of Christoffersen et al. (2011; RFS 2018)

claim: Wei-Zheng (J Banking & Finance 2010, individual equity options; sample period not stated in abstract): proportional spread is explained best by option return volatility (price elasticity times stock volatility); a maturity-substitution effect means short-term options can have smaller spreads than 60-90 day options when the latter are not listed in the expiration cycle.
quote: When medium-term options (60-90 days maturity) are not available, traders use short-term options as substitutes whose higher volume leads to a smaller bid-ask spread or better liquidity.
title: Trading activity and bid-ask spreads of individual equity options (abstract)

claim: Vendor ORATS (self-reported, practitioner; no sample stated): its backtester uses quotes 14 minutes before the close rather than closing quotes, and assumes slippage of 75% of bid-ask width for single-leg trades falling to 53% for four-leg spreads.
quote: We use a slippage of 75% of bid ask width for single legs all the way to 53% for four leg spreads.
title: ORATS backtesting methodology

claim: Harvey-Liu-Zhu (equity factor literature, tests from 1967 to ~2012; not options): because of repeated testing, a newly found factor needs a t-ratio above 3.0, not 2.0; framework allows correlated tests and missing data. Not options-specific.
quote: a newly discovered factor needs to clear a much higher hurdle, with a t-ratio greater than 3.0.
title: ... and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns (NBER w20592)

claim: Bajgrowicz-Scaillet (J Financial Economics 2012; Dow Jones index daily 1897-2011; technical trading rules, not options): false discovery rate control still could not pick ex ante the future best rules, and low transaction costs wiped out in-sample performance. Illustrates that selection among many tried rules fails out of sample once costs are charged.
quote: an investor would never have been able to select ex ante the future best-performing rules.
title: Technical trading revisited: False discoveries, persistence tests, and transaction costs

claim: Hjalmarsson (Fed IFDP 853, 2008; econometric theory, not options): with overlapping long-horizon observations, divide the standard t-statistic by the square root of the forecasting horizon rather than relying on autocorrelation-robust errors. For a 3-month hold sampled monthly or daily this implies a t of 3.0 becomes about 1.7 (horizon 3 in the sample's unit).
quote: the standard t-statistic can simply be divided by the square root of the forecasting horizon to correct for the effects of the overlap in the data
title: Inference in Long-Horizon Regressions (Hjalmarsson)

claim: McKeon (J Asset Management 2016; S&P 500 INDEX options, not single stock; bull call spread setups): spread returns are heavily affected by trading costs; long-volatility setups have positive skewness; setups with a short OTM call keep strong average returns after costs. Index comparison only; period not stated in abstract; full long-call-vs-spread comparison not read.
quote: Returns are heavily affected by costs of trading, but setups including short positions in out-the-money Calls return strong average returns even after costs.
title: Option spread trades: Returns on directional and volatility trades (abstract)

claim: FlashAlpha (vendor blog, self-reported): option archives that prune expired contracts cannot show a past chain, and universe studies excluding delisted companies measure survivors; distinguishes 'retained' (expired contracts and delisted names queryable) from 'survivorship-adjusted' (historical membership).
quote: a universe study that silently excludes companies that went away is measuring the survivors.
title: Point-in-Time Options Data: Why Most Options Backtests Are Optimistic
